AFRICAN RELIGION - THE WAY OF NATURAL AND SUPERNATURAL
(Full title: African Religion - the Way of Natural and Supernatural. The World of the Human meets the World of the Spirits.)
- This chapter begins Part 3 of the book: Other Living Religions.

OPENING QUOTE
- 'The African is notoriously religious.' - J. S. MBITI, Kenyan theologian.
- Meaning: religion runs through every part of African life.

INTRODUCTION AND OVERVIEW
- African religion is made up of complex and diverse traditions reflecting a rich cultural and spiritual heritage.
- In Africa there are AS MANY RELIGIONS AS THERE ARE COMMUNITIES.
- The COMMUNITY is seen as having the highest value.
- A community is made up of those who remember and share the tradition.
- The tradition is handed down, usually ORALLY (by word of mouth), from one generation to the next.
- THE ELDERS: their authority is final. They pass on the stories and practices they received. These have been shaped by the lived experience of the community over generations.

ORAL TRADITIONS
- Oral traditions: religious teaching passed on by word of mouth rather than in written scripture.
- They include: myths, epics, incantations, songs, spells, prayers and proverbs.
- They are part of religious rituals of movement and dance at altars or shrines, using symbols or objects considered sacred.
- African traditional religions have no written scriptures and no accounts of who founded them or how they developed. To study one fully you must look at it in the living context of its own society.

TRIBES AND WESTERN ATTITUDES
- Thousands of self-contained African tribes live on the continent, each with its own language and culture.
- Western colonial countries often arrogantly and judgementally dismissed African religion as primitive, superstitious 'mumbo-jumbo'.
- But thousands of tribal faiths still flourish and give communities meaningful, valued rituals and life-attitudes.
- The book suggests these tribal people may be MORE religious than many Western people.
- WHY? They live close to nature and are at the mercy of drought and flood, famine and disease, earthquake and storm. This makes them aware of human vulnerability and of the need to reach out to the creative power behind the natural world.
- Their religion is not expressed in ways familiar to Europeans: there are NO PRIESTHOODS, CREEDS OR TEMPLES.
- Faith is an integral part of life, with social and cultural expressions varying from tribe to tribe.
- Their experience of real human needs leads to a view of HUMAN NATURE as weak, defenceless and humble in the face of greater powers.
- Labels often used for such societies: 'primitive', 'simple', 'pre-literate', 'pre-industrial'. The book asks whether these reflect their deeply held beliefs.

BASIC FEATURES OF AFRICAN RELIGION (FOUND IN ALL RELIGIONS)
1. BELIEF IN A SPIRIT WORLD - MANA
- MANA: a spirit world or power behind all of life.
- Mana can be understood as spirits, friendly or antagonistic (hostile), to be praised or placated (calmed).
- They can also be gods of different parts of life, e.g. hunting or fertility.
- The visible and invisible parts of the universe link when spirits make their presence felt in nature, and when humans reach out to God in prayer and ritual.
- Many Africans believe in a CHIEF GOD or SUPREME BEING, who may be a personal being or a creative energy.
- They also accept LESSER GODS and/or NATURE SPIRITS who govern human activities and natural forces.
- These vary by the tribe's location: e.g. WATER SPIRITS for fisherfolk and tribes along rivers; HUNTING SPIRITS for tribes in forested areas.

2. ANCESTORS - THE 'LIVING DEAD'
- The 'living dead' are the spirits of the ancestors.
- They are honoured as PROTECTORS and GUIDES who can take prayers to the higher gods.
- Contact with ancestor spirits involves offerings, prayers and chants. It is an important part of family and community life.

3. NEW YEAR RITUALS
- Reinforce awareness of the need to reject the weaknesses and wrongs of life.
- In favour of a new resolution and a vision of better to come.
- This renewal comes from the great power behind all life.

4. PRAYERS AND MYTHS
- Prayers range from poetic epics on universal themes to individual daily requests for health and property, offered in the home to the GUARDIAN SPIRIT.
- Popular African myths: creation stories, animal fables, folk tales, heroic epics and legends - told at all levels of society.
- Myths deal with creation, death and suffering.
- They offer a divine-human link in the 'PERSON - UNIVERSE - SPIRIT' cycle.

5. SACRIFICE
- A hugely important ritual.
- Uses foodstuffs, animals, fowl, etc.
- Rules for the killing, pouring and burning are passed down through the generations.
- PURPOSES: to appease (calm) an offended god; to obtain a good harvest; to avert (prevent) a natural disaster; to honour a local god.
- Sacrifices can be INDIVIDUAL or COMMUNAL.

6. MEDICINE MEN AND WOMEN
- Found in every village.
- Roles: HEALER, DIVINER, MEDIUM; looking after the SHRINES; organising FESTIVALS.
- Respected for their knowledge of the medicinal properties of herbs and plants, for interpreting omens and signs, and for using prayer trances to understand the mysteries of the spirit world.

7. DREAMS AND VISIONS - DIVINATION
- Many tribes believe a person can be POSSESSED by a spirit, who controls their behaviour and speaks through them in a spirit language or in a dream.
- People consult others to interpret the message - a COMMAND, a WARNING or a REWARD.
- DIVINATION: interpreting messages from the spirit world. It is common and keeps contact with the spirit world real and vibrant.

HOW MANY AND WHERE?
- About 25 to 30 MILLION followers of African Traditional Religion in Africa today.
- Followers make up between ONE THIRD and ONE HALF of the population of: Benin, Botswana, Guinea-Bissau, Ivory Coast, Liberia, Madagascar, Mozambique and Sierra Leone.

LIFESTYLE OF BELIEVERS TODAY - RITES OF PASSAGE
- Every stage of life has religious aspects and can be marked by rituals. Four key transitional stages:
- BIRTH: naming and purifying rituals, with offerings of praise and thanks.
- INITIATION: rites for the young adult can involve physical hardship and emotional pressure to prepare them for adult responsibilities. Male and female circumcision remains a feature of many tribal initiations, but the MAIN AIM is to ensure knowledge of TRIBAL HISTORY and SOCIAL DUTIES.
- MARRIAGE: encouraged and expected. Children are seen as continuing (perpetuating) life and blessings. Each tribe has its own rituals.
- DEATH: funeral rites are observed very carefully so as not to offend the departed, who is journeying to the world of the spirits and the company of the ancestors. It is common to bury foodstuffs and tools/weapons with the dead, and to put up a shrine.

SACRED PLACES, OBJECTS AND MAGIC
- Sacred rites and objects are focal points of contact with the spirit world.
- Trees, mountains and springs can be sacred, depending on the spirit who lives there.
- Objects such as MASKS, DRUMS, STONES, FIRES and COLOURS become sacred by representing the presence of a spirit.
- MAGIC is commonly used for protection against evil spirits and hostile influences: from wearing jewellery with special powers to magical rites for banishing sickness or winning battles.

RELIGIOUS LEADERSHIP
- Ceremonies are regulated by people with certain powers or roles: elders, musicians, chiefs and kings, and spiritual intermediaries.
- Many roles are held within families; some are believed to be divinely appointed at random - another sign of spirit activity in the human world.

PERSECUTION / CONFLICT AND DIALOGUE
- African belief in the inseparable link between the visible and invisible worlds has produced a 'tapestry' of rituals and beliefs.
- These are NOT products of a primitive, magical, inferior culture but serious, meaningful responses to the search for a spiritual path that sustains people in life and death.
- For centuries Christian and Muslim missionaries tried to convert and educate Africans. Growing recognition of the value of traditional practice has opened some avenues of DIALOGUE.
- The demand for self-rule and 'AFRICA FOR AFRICANS' linked traditional religious practice with the struggle for INDEPENDENCE.
- Catholic missionaries since VATICAN II have successfully linked the gospel with the local culture.
- Many African churches now reinterpret the Christian vision of deeply held values: the SACREDNESS OF LIFE, the VALUE OF COMMUNITY and RESPECT FOR THE AFTERLIFE.
- Open question: is Christian or Muslim evangelism respectful of tribal beliefs and worship? Does it accept tribal religions as valid searches for meaning?

OTHER POINTS FROM THE ASSIGNMENTS
- Example tribes for case study: the Sudanese DINKA, the South African ZULU, the Nigerian YORUBA.
- SYNCRETISM: incorporating Christian and Muslim elements into African traditional religions. It has led to many new religious movements across Africa, as people adapt religion to their current experience.
- Traditional religions have NO MISSIONARY activity - they do not try to convert others.

KEY TERMS
- Oral traditions: beliefs, stories and practices passed on by word of mouth.
- Myths: stories (creation stories, fables, folk tales, epics, legends) dealing with creation, death and suffering.
- Rituals: religious actions of movement and dance at altars or shrines using sacred objects.
- Mana: the spirit world or power behind all of life.
- Ancestors: the 'living dead', honoured as protectors and guides who carry prayers to the higher gods.
- Sacrifice: offering food, animals or fowl to appease, ask or honour the gods.
- Medicine men and women: village healers, diviners and mediums who care for shrines and festivals.
- Divination: interpreting messages from the spirit world through dreams, visions, omens and possession.
- Initiation rites: rites preparing young adults for adult responsibilities and teaching tribal history and duties.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by oral tradition in African religion.
rows.model_answer: Oral tradition means the religion is passed on by word of mouth, not written scripture. Elders, whose authority is final, hand down myths, epics, incantations, songs, spells, prayers and proverbs from one generation to the next. These are used in rituals of movement and dance at altars or shrines.

rows.prompt: Describe African belief in the spirit world (Mana).
rows.model_answer: Mana is the power behind all of life, understood as spirits that can be friendly or hostile and must be praised or placated. Many Africans believe in a Chief God or Supreme Being, plus lesser gods and nature spirits who govern human activities and natural forces. These vary with location, such as water spirits for river tribes and hunting spirits for forest tribes.

rows.prompt: Who are the 'living dead' and how are they honoured?
rows.model_answer: The 'living dead' are the spirits of the ancestors. They are honoured as protectors and guides who can take people's prayers to the higher gods. People contact them through offerings, prayers and chants, which is an important part of family and community life.

rows.prompt: Give three purposes of sacrifice in African religion.
rows.model_answer: Sacrifice may be offered to appease an offended god, to obtain a good harvest, to avert a natural disaster or to honour a local god. Foodstuffs, animals and fowl are used, and sacrifices can be individual or communal.

rows.prompt: Describe the role of medicine men and women.
rows.model_answer: Medicine men and women are found in every village. They act as healers, diviners and mediums, look after the shrines and organise festivals. They are respected for their knowledge of medicinal herbs and plants, for interpreting omens and signs, and for using prayer trances to understand the spirit world.

rows.prompt: Name the four key rites of passage in African religion and give one detail of each.
rows.model_answer: Birth involves naming and purifying rituals with offerings of praise and thanks. Initiation prepares young adults for adult responsibilities, sometimes with hardship or circumcision, mainly to teach tribal history and duties. Marriage is expected and children are seen as continuing life and blessings. At death, careful funeral rites avoid offending the departed, and food and tools are often buried with them.

rows.prompt: How have Catholic missionaries since Vatican II approached African culture?
rows.model_answer: Since Vatican II, Catholic missionaries have linked the gospel message with the culture of the people receiving it. Many African churches now reinterpret the Christian vision of values Africans already hold deeply: the sacredness of life, the value of community and respect for the afterlife. The chapter still asks whether such evangelism truly respects tribal beliefs as valid searches for meaning.

rows.prompt: Outline the main beliefs and features of African traditional religion.
rows.model_answer:
African traditional religion is not one religion: there are as many religions as there are communities. It is passed on orally by the elders through myths, songs, prayers and proverbs, and it has no priesthoods, creeds or temples.

First, Africans believe in a spirit world or power behind all life, called Mana. Spirits may be friendly or hostile and must be praised or placated. Many believe in a Chief God or Supreme Being, together with lesser gods and nature spirits, such as water spirits for river tribes and hunting spirits for forest tribes.

Second, the ancestors, or 'living dead', are honoured as protectors and guides who carry prayers to the higher gods, through offerings, prayers and chants.

Third, sacrifice of foodstuffs, animals and fowl is hugely important, to appease an offended god, gain a good harvest, avert disaster or honour a local god.

Fourth, medicine men and women in every village act as healers, diviners and mediums, using herbs, omens and prayer trances.

Finally, dreams and visions matter: a person may be possessed by a spirit, and divination interprets the message as a command, warning or reward. New Year rituals and myths about creation, death and suffering also link the person, universe and spirit.

May refer to: diversity and community; oral tradition and elders; no priesthoods/creeds/temples; Mana, Supreme Being, lesser gods and nature spirits; ancestors as 'living dead'; New Year rituals; prayers and myths; sacrifice and its purposes; medicine men and women; dreams, possession and divination. Credit 4-5 well-developed features.

rows.prompt: Describe how African traditional religion marks the stages of life.
rows.model_answer:
To African people every stage of life has religious aspects, but four transitional stages are especially important.

At birth there are naming and purifying rituals, with offerings of praise and thanks.

Initiation rites for young adults can involve physical hardships and emotional pressures to prepare them for adult responsibilities. Male and female circumcision is still a feature of many tribal initiations, but the main aim is to make sure the young person knows the tribe's history and their social duties.

Marriage is encouraged and expected, and children are seen as continuing life and blessings. Each tribe has its own rituals to mark the union.

At death, funeral rites are observed very carefully so as not to offend the departed, who is journeying to the world of the spirits and the company of the ancestors. It is common to bury food and tools or weapons with the dead and to put up a shrine. These rituals show the close link between the human world and the world of the spirits.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 8-10, good 5-7, fair 0-4. Award up to 2.5 marks per stage (birth, initiation, marriage, death) for accurate detail: naming/purifying and offerings; hardships, circumcision, tribal history and duties; marriage expected, children as blessing; careful funeral rites, journey to ancestors, burial of food and tools, shrine.

rows.prompt: Explain the role of medicine men and women and of divination in African religion.
rows.model_answer:
Medicine men and women are found in every village and are central to religious life. They act as healers, diviners and mediums. They look after the shrines and organise the festivals. They are respected for their knowledge of the medicinal properties of herbs and plants, for interpreting omens and signs, and for using prayer trances to understand the mysteries of the spirit world.

Divination is the interpreting of messages from the spirit world. Many tribes believe that a person can be possessed by a spirit, which controls their behaviour and speaks through them in a spirit language or in a dream. People consult others to interpret the message, which may be a command, a warning or a reward. Divination is common, and it keeps contact with the spirit world real and vibrant for people. Both show the African belief that the visible and invisible worlds are closely linked.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 8-10, good 5-7, fair 0-4. Medicine men and women up to 5 marks (healer, diviner, medium, shrines, festivals, herbs, omens, trances). Divination up to 5 marks (possession, spirit language, dreams, interpretation as command/warning/reward, keeps spirit contact real).

rows.prompt: 'Far from being the products of a primitive, magical, inferior culture...' Discuss the challenges facing African traditional religion today and its relationship with other religions.
rows.model_answer:
For centuries Western colonial countries arrogantly dismissed African religion as primitive, superstitious 'mumbo-jumbo'. The chapter argues that its rituals and beliefs are serious and meaningful responses to the search for a spiritual path that sustains people in life and death. Thousands of tribal faiths still flourish, with about 25 to 30 million followers, making up a third to a half of the population in countries such as Benin, Liberia and Mozambique.

One challenge has been centuries of Christian and Muslim missionary work aimed at converting and educating Africans. Growing recognition of the value of traditional religion has opened some avenues of dialogue. The demand for self-rule and 'Africa for Africans' also linked traditional religious practice with the struggle for independence.

Since Vatican II, Catholic missionaries have linked the gospel to local culture, and many African churches now reinterpret Christian values that Africans already hold: the sacredness of life, the value of community and respect for the afterlife. Syncretism, mixing Christian and Muslim elements into traditional religion, has created many new religious movements.

The question remains whether Christian or Muslim evangelism respects tribal beliefs and worship, and accepts tribal religions as valid searches for meaning. Unlike those faiths, traditional religions do not try to convert others.

May refer to: colonial dismissal as 'mumbo-jumbo'; religion as serious response to spiritual quest; numbers and countries; missionary work by Christianity and Islam; dialogue; 'Africa for Africans' and independence; post-Vatican II linking of gospel and culture, shared values (sacredness of life, community, afterlife); syncretism and new movements; question of respect for tribal religion; no missionary activity in traditional religions.
